claims.text: The starting material is a eutectic high-entropy alloy with hierarchical dual-phase lamellar colonies, exemplified by FCC/L12 and B2 phases.
Cold rolling followed by tailored annealing can adjust lamellar spacing and colony alignment.
The desired processed architecture has increased lamellar spacing and aligned colonies.
Increased lamellar spacing and favorable colony orientation provide extended pathways for dislocations to bypass internal boundaries.
The adjusted lamellar architecture reduces dislocation pile-ups at internal lamellar boundaries.
Reducing dislocation pile-ups lowers local stress concentrations.
Lower local stress concentrations prevent or mitigate early microcrack nucleation during room-temperature tensile deformation.
Back-stress hardening arising from a heterogeneous hierarchical microstructure can delay necking and improve the strength-ductility combination.
The proposed processing route will increase tensile elongation relative to the untreated material.
The proposed processing route will retain or modestly increase yield strength and ultimate tensile strength relative to the untreated material.
Cryo-rolling and annealing previously produced simultaneous increases in strength and ductility in a lamellar AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy.
The untreated alloy exhibits significant dislocation pile-up at internal lamellar boundaries, limited ductility, and premature microcracking under room-temperature tensile loading.
The proposed enhancement is applicable under room-temperature uniaxial tensile conditions.
Excessive coarsening or colony misalignment would eliminate beneficial dislocation redistribution and could reduce strength.
The magnitude of strength and ductility improvement depends on rolling reduction, annealing temperature, and annealing time.
A same-material processed-versus-untreated control experiment can test changes in elongation, strength, pile-ups, and microcracking.
